BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN) -- The commander of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia's Force 47 told reporters in Bogota Monday -- a day after surrendering -- that "the solution is not through war. There must be dialogue." Nelly Avila Moreno, center, alias Karina, is escorted by soldiers after surrendering. Nelly Avila Moreno, 45, whose nom de guerre was Karina, said she and her longtime male companion made the decision jointly to abandon the FARC group, based in the jungle, at 5 a.m. Sunday. She said pressure from Colombian soldiers had been key to their decision, and she called on her fellow rebels to follow her example. "I invite them to change the sensibility that is among the guerrillas," she said, seated by her companion, who said nothing during the news conference. She also had a message for the Colombian people: "It is important to do something for peace in Colombia, and that need to do something is precisely one of my motivations." After 24 years with the FARC, Karina said she wants to reintegrate with society. "At this moment, what I am thinking about is reuniting with my family and with all of society," she said. Karina said she had had no contact with the group's leaders for the past two years. During that time, she said, "I was trying to stay alive." She said she knows nothing about the group's leaders, because "everything in the FARC is very compartmentalized." Still, she did hear through the news media about the killing by another member of FARC of Ivan Rios, a member of the group's central high command. "We suffered a very strong blow," she said. She acknowledged that news led her to worry about the possibility that one of her fellow guerrillas might consider doing the same thing to her. "A person has a lot of combatants alongside, but you don't know what each one is thinking," she said. Asked about news reports of guerrilla operations she may have participated in, Karina admitted to nothing. "They accuse me of a lot of things I wasn't part of," she said. But Miguel Antonio Paez told CNN en Espanol that he remembers well the woman who, with a band of guerrillas, stopped the bus he was on in 2004 in northwest Colombia, ordered him and the other passengers off and the bus be burned. "The commander of that guerrilla group -- a dark-haired woman, tall, with one eye missing -- called herself Karina," he said. "She ordered me tied up. Here, I have the marks from the wires, and there, while I was tied up, she lopped off my penis and testicles and I remained castrated for all my life." Asked specifically about the killing of the father of President Alvaro Uribe in 1983, she said she did not know who carried out the act, and added, "I don't have my hands stained in that deed." She said that with her surrender have come new fears about possible retribution from FARC loyalists, who consider her a traitor. Wearing a red sweatshirt and what appeared to be a diamond earring in her left ear, she said she once believed the FARC would rule Colombia. "I once dreamed of that," she said. Gen. Mario Montoya, chief of the army, said two Colombian air force helicopters were sent Sunday to pick up Karina and her companion, who had given authorities their general location. "With this, we have given a confounding strike to the FARC structure," particularly to Front 47, which at this point is practically dismantled," he said. Since the killing of Rios, 45 members of the group have laid down their arms and accepted a government plan for reinstallation into society, he said. "We want to send a message to all members of FARC who persist in the mountains," he said. "To tell them, what Karina has done is the road all the members of FARC should go down. If they don't, we are going to continue combating them. Today, more than ever, I invite them to lay down their arms, take the plan. We don't want them dead. We want them alive."

outputs.L1:
BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN) -- The commander of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia's Front 47 told reporters in Bogota on Monday—one day after her surrender—that "the solution does not lie in war. There must be dialogue."

Nelly Avila Moreno, 45, known by her nom de guerre "Karina," was escorted by soldiers following her surrender. She explained that she and her longtime male companion had jointly decided to abandon the jungle-based FARC organization at 5 a.m. Sunday. She credited sustained pressure from Colombian soldiers as a decisive factor in their choice, and urged her fellow rebels to follow suit.

"I invite them to reconsider the mindset that prevails among the guerrillas," she said, seated beside her companion, who remained silent throughout the news conference. She also offered a message to the Colombian people: "It is essential to work toward peace in Colombia, and that conviction is precisely one of my motivations."

After 24 years with the FARC, Karina expressed a desire to reintegrate into society. "At this moment, what I am thinking about is reuniting with my family and with society as a whole," she said.

Karina noted that she had had no contact with the organization's leadership for the past two years. "I was focused on staying alive," she explained, adding that she remained unaware of the leadership's activities because "everything within the FARC is highly compartmentalized." Nevertheless, she learned through news reports of the killing of Ivan Rios—a member of the group's central command—by a fellow FARC member. "It was a severe blow to us," she said, acknowledging that the incident heightened her own fears that a comrade might turn against her in similar fashion. "You have many combatants around you, but you never truly know what each one is thinking," she said.

When questioned about alleged guerrilla operations she may have participated in, Karina denied any involvement. "I am accused of many things I had no part in," she said.

However, Miguel Antonio Paez offered a starkly different account to CNN en Español, recalling vividly the woman who, alongside a band of guerrillas, stopped the bus he was riding in 2004 in northwestern Colombia, forced the passengers off, and ordered the vehicle burned. "The commander of that guerrilla unit—a tall woman with dark hair, missing one eye—identified herself as Karina," he said. "She had me bound. I still bear the scars from the wires. And while I was restrained, she cut off my penis and testicles, leaving me castrated for life."

Asked directly about the 1983 killing of the father of President Álvaro Uribe, Karina said she did not know who was responsible, adding, "My hands are not stained by that act."

She acknowledged that her surrender had introduced new fears of retaliation from FARC loyalists who now regard her as a traitor. Dressed in a red sweatshirt and wearing what appeared to be a diamond earring in her left ear, she reflected on her past convictions: "I once dreamed the FARC would govern Colombia."

Gen. Mario Montoya, commander of the Colombian army, confirmed that two air force helicopters were dispatched Sunday to retrieve Karina and her companion after they disclosed their general location to authorities. "With this, we have dealt a devastating blow to the FARC's structure," he said, "particularly to Front 47, which is now virtually dismantled."

Montoya noted that since the killing of Rios, 45 FARC members have laid down their arms and accepted a government reintegration program. "We want to send a message to all FARC members who remain in the mountains," he said. "What Karina has done is the path every member of the FARC should follow. If they do not, we will continue to fight them. Today, more than ever, I urge them to lay down their weapons and accept this plan. We do not want them dead—we want them alive."

Regarding the 1983 murder of President Alvaro Uribe's father, Karina claimed no knowledge of who committed the crime, stating, "My hands are not stained by that particular act."

# Notorious FARC Commander Surrenders, Calls for Peace

Nelly Avila Moreno, better known by her nom de guerre "Karina," a commander of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia's (FARC) Force 47, turned herself in to Colombian authorities on Sunday, bringing an end to her 24-year tenure with the rebel organization. The following day, she addressed reporters in Bogota, offering insight into her decision and her hopes for the future of her country.

During the press conference, Karina made a passionate appeal for peace, declaring unequivocally that war cannot resolve Colombia's decades-long internal conflict. She insisted that dialogue and negotiation, rather than continued armed struggle, represent the only viable path forward for a nation weary of violence.

Karina disclosed that the decision to abandon the FARC was not made alone but was reached jointly with her longtime companion. She acknowledged that mounting pressure from Colombian military forces played a significant role in pushing the couple toward this life-altering choice, suggesting that the increasing effectiveness of government operations against the guerrillas had made continued resistance increasingly untenable.

Looking ahead, Karina spoke of her hopes to reintegrate into civilian society and reconnect with family members from whom she had long been separated during her years in the jungle with the rebel group. She extended a direct appeal to her former comrades still fighting within FARC's ranks, urging them to follow her lead and lay down their arms in the interest of achieving lasting peace for Colombia.

In a particularly revealing portion of her remarks, Karina described the extent of her isolation within the organization, stating she had had no communication with FARC's central leadership for a full two years—a consequence of the group's rigorously compartmentalized command structure designed to protect the organization from infiltration and capture. She also admitted to a deep sense of personal fear that had taken hold following the assassination of Ivan Rios, a member of FARC's central command who was killed by one of his own subordinates. This incident, she confessed, left her apprehensive that she might meet a similar fate at the hands of someone within her own ranks, underscoring the climate of distrust and paranoia that had come to pervade the organization's internal dynamics.

# The Fall of Karina: A FARC Commander's Journey from War to Surrender

After more than two decades of guerrilla warfare, Nelly Avila Moreno—better known by her nom de guerre "Karina"—made the momentous decision to lay down her arms and surrender to Colombian authorities, bringing to an end a 24-year career as one of the most recognized commanders within the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC). Her surrender marks not merely the exit of a mid-level fighter, but the departure of a woman who had risen through the ranks to become one of the most visible female leaders in Latin America's longest-running insurgency.

Moreno's decision to abandon the armed struggle was shaped by a combination of factors, both tactical and deeply personal. On one hand, she cited the intensifying military pressure that Colombian security forces had been exerting on FARC units throughout the country. Years of sustained government offensives, improved intelligence capabilities, and coordinated military campaigns had steadily eroded the guerrilla group's operational capacity, making the daily reality of jungle warfare increasingly untenable for commanders like Karina. The constant threat of capture or death, combined with the group's shrinking resources and diminishing strategic options, had transformed what was once a viable revolutionary path into a precarious and increasingly hopeless existence.

Beyond the military calculus, however, Moreno spoke to something more profound: a personal yearning for peace and an end to the cycle of violence that had defined her adult life. After dedicating nearly a quarter-century to armed conflict, she expressed a desire to pursue reconciliation rather than continue down a path of endless confrontation. This sentiment reflects a broader psychological and ideological shift that many long-serving guerrilla fighters experience after years of combat—a recognition that the human costs of perpetual war may outweigh whatever political objectives once justified taking up arms.

The timing and symbolism of Karina's surrender carry substantial weight within the context of FARC's evolving internal dynamics. Her departure came shortly after the killing of Ivan Rios, a member of FARC's central command and secretariat, whose death represented a significant blow to the organization's senior leadership structure. Rios was killed under circumstances that further underscored the vulnerabilities within FARC's command hierarchy, adding to a mounting sense of crisis at the highest levels of the organization.

Together, these events—the loss of a central command member and the voluntary surrender of a prominent field commander—paint a picture of an organization increasingly beset by internal strain, declining morale, and fracturing loyalty among its ranks. For decades, FARC had projected an image of ideological cohesion and military resilience, but developments like these suggested that such unity was becoming harder to sustain. The combination of external military pressure and internal disintegration created a feedback loop: as the group's position weakened, more commanders and fighters began questioning whether continued armed struggle served any viable purpose.

Karina's surrender, in particular, resonated deeply within Colombian society and among international observers tracking the conflict. As a woman who had achieved significant command responsibilities within a historically male-dominated insurgent structure, her exit carried symbolic weight beyond simple attrition statistics. It signaled to other FARC members—particularly those who may have been wavering in their commitment—that surrender was not only possible but could be framed as a path toward personal redemption and national reconciliation rather than mere defeat or betrayal.

For the Colombian government, her surrender represented a valuable propaganda and psychological victory in the broader campaign to dismantle FARC through a combination of military pressure and incentives for demobilization. Each high-profile defection reinforced the narrative that the insurgency was crumbling from within, encouraging further defections while simultaneously demoralizing remaining combatants who might have been contemplating their own futures within the organization.

Ultimately, the story of Karina's surrender encapsulates the broader trajectory of FARC during this period: an organization caught between its revolutionary origins and an increasingly untenable present, where military setbacks, leadership losses, and individual moral reckonings converged to accelerate its decline. Her journey from feared commander to civilian seeking peace serves as a microcosm of the larger societal shift occurring across Colombia, as the nation slowly moved toward the possibility of ending one of the hemisphere's most protracted armed conflicts.

# Bogotá: Colombia's High-Altitude Capital

Bogotá, the capital city of Colombia, sits at an elevation of roughly 2,640 meters (8,660 feet) above sea level, making it one of the highest major cities in the world. Nestled in the Andes mountains on a plateau known as the Bogotá savanna, the city serves as the political, economic, and cultural heart of the nation.

## A City of Contrasts

With a metropolitan population exceeding 10 million people, Bogotá represents the full spectrum of Colombian society. Modern skyscrapers in the financial district stand alongside colonial-era architecture in La Candelaria, the historic city center where cobblestone streets wind past centuries-old churches and colorful buildings.

The city has undergone significant transformation in recent decades, shifting from a place once associated primarily with security concerns to a vibrant destination for business, culture, and tourism. International media outlets, including CNN, have covered this evolution extensively, reporting on everything from Colombia's peace process and economic development to Bogotá's emergence as a hub for innovation, art, and gastronomy in Latin America.

## Cultural and Economic Significance

Bogotá hosts numerous world-class museums, including the Gold Museum (Museo del Oro), which houses one of the world's largest collections of pre-Columbian gold artifacts. The city's Botero Museum showcases works by Colombia's famous artist Fernando Botero, offering free admission to visitors.

As Colombia's primary economic engine, Bogotá attracts international investment and has developed a growing reputation as a startup hub in the region. News coverage from major networks has highlighted the city's efforts to address urban challenges while capitalizing on its strengths in education, with numerous universities drawing students from across Latin America.

## Looking Forward

Today's Bogotá continues to navigate the balance between preserving its rich history and embracing modernization, making it a frequently discussed subject in international news coverage examining Colombia's broader development and its role in South American affairs.

# FARC Commander "Karina" Surrenders in Blow to Colombian Rebels

**BOGOTÁ, COLOMBIA** — In a significant development in Colombia's decades-long internal conflict, Nelly Ávila Moreno, better known by her nom de guerre "Karina," one of the most senior female commanders in the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), turned herself in to government forces this week, ending a guerrilla career spanning more than two decades.

Karina, who led the FARC's 47th Front in the mountainous Antioquia region, had a bounty of hundreds of thousands of dollars on her head and was wanted in connection with numerous kidnappings, killings, and attacks attributed to the rebel group. Colombian officials described her surrender as one of the most important defections in the movement's history.

## "I Am Tired of War"

At a press conference following her surrender, a visibly emotional Karina addressed reporters, asking forgiveness from her victims and calling on remaining rebels to lay down their arms.

"I am tired of this war that has brought nothing but pain to Colombian families — including my own," she said. "I ask forgiveness from all those I have harmed, directly or indirectly. I did not have another way out for many years, but today I choose peace."

She confirmed she had been in secret contact with military intelligence for weeks before her surrender and cited disillusionment with FARC leadership and the physical toll of jungle warfare — she has a permanent facial injury from a firefight — as reasons for leaving the movement.

"The FARC I joined as a young woman does not exist anymore," she added. "It has become something else — something I no longer recognize."

## Military Hails "Major Victory"

Colombian Defense Minister officials and army commanders quickly held their own briefings, framing Karina's surrender as validation of the government's hardline security policy and its campaign to weaken FARC's command structure through both military pressure and incentives for desertion.

"This sends an unmistakable message to the remaining FARC leadership: the state's arms are open to those who want peace, but our forces will not relent against those who continue in armed struggle," a senior army general told reporters at a joint briefing.

Officials said Karina's detailed knowledge of FARC operations, logistics routes, and personnel in the Antioquia region could yield significant intelligence gains.

## Mixed Reactions From Victims

Reaction among victims' families and human rights advocates was more complicated. Some expressed cautious relief, while others voiced anger that Karina would likely receive a reduced sentence under Colombia's demobilization framework in exchange for cooperation and confession.

"My son was killed by her front. No apology brings him back," one relative of a victim told local media outside the press conference venue, declining to give her name. "But if her surrender means fewer families suffer what we did, then some good has come of it."

Human rights organizations called for full accountability, urging that any leniency be conditioned on complete disclosure of crimes, including alleged killings and forced recruitment of minors attributed to her front.

## Broader Implications

Analysts say Karina's defection — following other high-profile FARC surrenders and defections in recent years — reflects mounting internal pressure on the guerrilla group amid sustained military operations and fracturing morale among its ranks.

Whether her surrender accelerates further defections or peace negotiations remains to be seen, but for many Colombians weary after decades of conflict, it represents another small, symbolic crack in an insurgency that has shaped the nation's modern history.

*This is a developing story.*

**BOGOTA, Colombia** — One of the most notorious commanders in Colombia's leftist FARC guerrilla movement turned herself in to government forces this week, marking what military officials are calling a significant blow to the rebel group's eastern operations.

Nelly Avila Moreno, better known by her nom de guerre "Karina," commanded the FARC's 47th Front for years and had a bounty on her head reportedly worth hundreds of thousands of dollars. Colombian authorities have long accused her of orchestrating kidnappings, extortion schemes, and attacks that terrorized rural communities in the Antioquia region.

"I am tired of this war," Moreno told reporters shortly after her surrender. "I want to ask forgiveness from all the people I have hurt. I want a chance to be with my daughter and to live a normal life, away from the jungle."

Moreno, who reportedly lost an eye in combat years ago, is one of the highest-ranking female commanders to abandon the FARC's ranks since Colombia's government began offering demobilization incentives to rebel fighters.

## Villagers Recall Years of Terror

For residents in the areas Karina once controlled, her surrender brings a complicated mix of relief and lingering trauma.

"She was ruthless," said one farmer from a rural township in Antioquia, who spoke on condition of anonymity out of fear of reprisals from remaining FARC members. "They took my brother in the night. We never learned exactly what happened to him. People disappeared. Livestock was stolen, homes were burned if you didn't cooperate. When we heard her name, we were afraid."

Human rights groups have documented numerous accusations against Karina's front, including forced recruitment of minors and violent reprisals against suspected informants — allegations Moreno has not directly addressed in her public statements since surrendering.

## Military Calls it a "Major Victory"

Gen. Mario Montoya, commander of Colombia's army, characterized Moreno's surrender as evidence that the government's sustained military pressure on the FARC is working.

"This is another clear sign that the FARC is weakening from within," Montoya said at a press briefing. "Karina was a symbol of terror in that region for years. Her decision to abandon the armed struggle shows that even the most hardened commanders understand the group's cause is lost. We will continue this pressure until peace is achieved."

Montoya added that Colombian forces would continue offering demobilization pathways to other rebel commanders, framing the strategy as central to President Álvaro Uribe's broader security agenda.

## Reintegration Ahead

Moreno is expected to enter Colombia's reincorporation program, which offers reduced sentences and support services to former combatants who demobilize, provided they confess to crimes and cooperate with authorities.

Her case is likely to draw scrutiny from victims' organizations demanding accountability, even as the government touts her departure from the battlefield as a symbolic turning point in the decades-long conflict.

The FARC, founded in 1964, has seen its numbers dwindle in recent years amid military offensives and a wave of desertions, though the group continues to control territory in remote parts of the country.

*CNN's Bogota bureau contributed to this report.*
